sermon:
## A Genealogy of Sinners and the God Who Kept His Word
*How the Gospel begins with a list of names you would have left out*

**Text:** Matthew 1–2 · **Supporting:** Genesis 12:1–3 · 2 Samuel 7:12–16 · Isaiah 7:14 · Hosea 11:1

Matthew begins the story of Jesus the way no editor would. He begins with a list. Seventeen verses of fathers and sons before a single thing happens, and most of us read past it the way we read past the credits. We should not. Because the first thing Matthew wants us to know about Jesus is not that he was holy. It is that he came through us.

**The list God was not ashamed to keep**

"The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Two names anchor the whole register, and both are promises. To Abraham God had said, "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:3). To David he had sworn, "I will raise up your offspring after you... and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:12). Matthew is telling us the genealogy is not biology. It is fidelity. God making good on words spoken centuries before the people who heard them were dust.

Then look at who is in the line. Tamar, who played the harlot with her father-in-law. Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute. Ruth, a Moabite outsider whom the law kept at arm's length. Bathsheba, named here only as "the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6)—the wound of David's adultery left in the record on purpose. We would have scrubbed this. We would have built a pedigree. God built a confession. The Messiah comes through liars and outsiders and the wreckage of a king's worst night, and the line is not weakened by them. It is carried by them.

**Immanuel—the name that changes the account**

Then the virgin. "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (Matthew 1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14). The genealogy runs father to father, begot and begot, forty generations of human cause and effect—and then it stops. Joseph does not beget. "Mary, of whom Jesus was born" (Matthew 1:16). The chain of men breaks, because at the decisive point the work is not ours. We supplied the sin. God supplied the Son.

And the name. Immanuel—God with us. Not God watching us. Not God instructing us from a safe distance. God with us, inside the list, inside the family, inside the mess we made. The other name the angel gives is just as exact: "you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). Not save them from Rome. Not save them from poverty. From their sins. The diagnosis is named before the cure, and the cure is a person.

Slow down on Bathsheba, because the way Matthew names her is the whole gospel in a single phrase. He does not write "Bathsheba." He writes that David was the father of Solomon "by the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6). The genealogy will not let David forget. It keeps the murdered man's name in the record beside the king who arranged his death, so that every generation reading the line of the Messiah has to read past the worst thing David ever did. We bury our Uriahs. We tell the version of the story where we come out clean. God put Uriah's name in the family tree of his Son and left it there, because the Christ who came to save us from our sins was never going to pretend we did not have any.

Then chapter two darkens. Magi come asking for the King, and a king named Herod hears "King" and reaches for a sword. "He sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem" (Matthew 2:16). The world's first response to the true King is to try to murder him in his crib. And the holy family flees to Egypt, so that the word might be fulfilled, "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Matthew 2:15, citing Hosea 11:1). Watch what Matthew is doing. He is putting Jesus exactly where Israel was—down in Egypt, called out by God—so that this Son can do what that son could not.

**We are the genealogy he was not ashamed of**

Here is where it lands, and it lands on us. We read the list of sinners as ancient history, as if we are reading about other people. We are not. I have stood in a pulpit and quietly curated my own genealogy—mentioned the seminary, left out the years I was an angry man who did not believe in the God I was furious at. We all keep two lists. The one we present and the one that is true. And the gospel begins by refusing the presentable one. God wrote the true list into the front of the book and signed his Son's name at the bottom of it.

That is the mercy, and it costs you the version of yourself you have been protecting. The Christ did not come through people who had it together. He came through Tamar and Rahab and Bathsheba's grief, because he was always coming for people exactly like them. Exactly like you. The name is Immanuel. He did not stay where it was clean.

And this is why the two names the angel gives matter in the order they come. First the work: "you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). Then the presence: "they shall call his name Immanuel" (Matthew 1:23). He saves from sin so that he can be with us—because sin was the wall, and until the wall came down, God-with-us was a sentence of terror rather than mercy. A holy God in the room with unholy people is bad news, not good, unless the sin is dealt with first. So Jesus saves, and then Immanuel becomes the most comforting word in the Bible instead of the most frightening one. The genealogy of sinners ends in the only name that makes their nearness to God survivable.

So the promise to Abraham, four thousand years old, and the promise to David, a thousand years old, and the ache of every parent who buried a child in Bethlehem, all converge on a manger no king would have chosen. We kept failing the covenant. He kept it himself. And he wrote our names in the line, not to shame us, but because a Savior who only saved the worthy would have saved no one at all.

God kept the promise himself.

## The Son Who Stood Where the Son Had Fallen
*Baptism, beloved-ness, and forty days in the wilderness*

**Text:** Matthew 3–4:11 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 8:2–3 · Exodus 4:22 · Isaiah 42:1 · Deuteronomy 6:13, 16

Before Jesus does a single miracle, before he calls a disciple or preaches a sentence, Matthew puts him in two places. The water and the wilderness. He is named at the one and tested in the other, and you cannot understand the gospel until you see that the testing comes immediately after the naming. That order is not an accident. That order is the whole Christian life.

**The voice from heaven before the work begins**

John the Baptist is in the desert, dressed like Elijah, preaching the oldest word in the prophets: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matthew 3:2). And Jesus comes to be baptized. John resists—rightly. Why would the sinless one stand in a line for sinners? Jesus answers, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15). He gets in our line. From the first public moment he stands with sinners, not above them.

And then heaven opens. "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). The Father echoes Isaiah—"Behold my servant... my chosen, in whom my soul delights" (Isaiah 42:1). Notice when the Father says it. Before the ministry. Before the cross. Before one thing has been accomplished. The beloved-ness is not earned by the work. It is the ground the work stands on. Jesus does not go into the wilderness to become the Son. He goes in as the Son.

**The wilderness Israel failed, the Son passed**

"Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil" (Matthew 4:1). Forty days. The number is a sermon by itself. Israel had forty years in a wilderness, and God told them why: "that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2). God had called Israel "my firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22). And that son failed every test. Hungry, they grumbled. Thirsty, they doubted. Frightened, they built a golden calf and went looking for security in something they could see.

Now the true Son is in the same wilderness, facing the same three pressures, and watch how he fights. He does not argue. He does not negotiate. Three times he answers with Deuteronomy—the very book of Israel's failure—turned now into the weapon of the Son's obedience. "Man shall not live by bread alone" (Matthew 4:4, from Deuteronomy 8:3). "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7, from Deuteronomy 6:16). "You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve" (Matthew 4:10, from Deuteronomy 6:13). Where Israel was hungry and grasped, the Son was hungry and trusted. Where Israel demanded a sign, the Son refused one. Where Israel bowed to a calf for safety, the Son refused all the kingdoms of the world rather than bow to the one offering them.

The tempter even quotes Scripture back at him in the second test, and Jesus does not take the bait of a verse ripped from its purpose. The devil can recite the Bible. He cannot obey it. That is the difference, and it is the whole difference.

Look closer at the first temptation, because it is the one that exposes us. "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread" (Matthew 4:3). The trap is in the word "if." The Father has just said "this is my beloved Son," and the enemy comes immediately to put a question mark where God put a period. Are you really? Then prove it. Use the power. Feed yourself. And Jesus refuses to manufacture from his own hand what the Father had not yet given. "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). Israel in the wilderness had the manna and still doubted the God who sent it. The Son had nothing but the word of his Father and trusted it through forty days of hunger. That is what obedience looks like when it costs something. Not a feeling. A man saying no to bread because his Father has not said yes.

**The Son stood so that you, who fall, would have a place to stand**

Now turn it around, because this is not finally a story about willpower. We read this and reach for the lesson: resist temptation, memorize verses, try harder. But you have tried harder. So have I. I have fasted from a sin on Sunday and returned to it by Thursday, and the wilderness of my own heart has won more rounds than I will admit from a pulpit. If the point of this passage is that you should be like Jesus in the desert, the passage is bad news, because you are like Israel. So am I.

Here is the gospel hiding in the obedience. The beloved Son stood in the place where the firstborn son fell—and he did it for the firstborn son. His perfect obedience is not merely an example held over your head. It is a righteousness held out to your empty hands. He passed the test you keep failing, and then he walked that obedience all the way to a cross to give it to you. The voice that said "my beloved Son" over the sinless one is the voice that says "beloved" over you—not because you stood, but because he did.

So you go into your own wilderness this week already named. The pressure is real. The bread is real, the fear is real, the kingdoms the enemy offers look like security every time. But you do not enter the desert to win your Father's approval. You enter it as one already approved, in a Son who never lost a round.

Where Israel fell, the Son stood.

## A Righteousness That Starts Where No One Can See
*The blessed life and the heart the King came to remake*

**Text:** Matthew 4:12–7:12 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 9:1–2 · Psalm 24:3–4 · Jeremiah 31:33 · Ezekiel 36:26

Jesus opens his mouth on a mountain and the first word out of it is not a command. It is a blessing. And the blessing goes to all the wrong people. "Blessed are the poor in spirit... blessed are those who mourn... blessed are the meek" (Matthew 5:3–5). Not the strong. Not the certain. Not the ones who have arrived. The bankrupt. We have spent so long sanding the Sermon on the Mount into good advice that we have missed that it begins by congratulating the people we pity.

**The kingdom dawns on people sitting in the dark**

Matthew sets the scene with Isaiah. Jesus moves to Galilee, and "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light" (Matthew 4:16, quoting Isaiah 9:2). Then comes the announcement that organizes everything after it: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matthew 4:17). The kingdom is not a place you go when you die. It is a reign breaking in now, and the first thing it does is call ordinary fishermen off their boats. "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:19). They left the nets immediately. Not because they understood. Because the King called.

And then the mountain. Matthew is putting Jesus where Moses stood, giving the law of the kingdom from the height the way the law came from Sinai—except this King does not carry the tablets. He is the one who wrote them.

**Righteousness that the Pharisees could not fake**

Here is the line that should stop every religious person cold: "unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:20). The Pharisees were the most rigorous people alive. They tithed their spice racks. And Jesus says you have to be more righteous than them—then spends the rest of the chapter showing you what he means, and it is not more rules. It is the heart under the rule.

"You have heard that it was said... 'You shall not murder'... But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable" (Matthew 5:21–22). You have not committed adultery? "Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:27–28). He keeps driving the law inward, past the hands, past the record, into the place no one can audit. The Pharisee cleaned the outside of the cup. The King wants the inside. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8)—and the psalmist already asked who can ascend God's hill, and answered, "he who has clean hands and a pure heart" (Psalm 24:4). Clean hands you can manage. A pure heart you cannot manufacture.

This is why the Sermon on the Mount is not, finally, a ladder. Read honestly, it is a mirror. Anger is murder. Lust is adultery. A grudging dollar is not generosity. If the standard is the heart, then every one of us has already broken it before breakfast, and the most disciplined religious life in the room cannot reach it from the outside.

And then Jesus raises the standard past anything human striving could reach. "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you... You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:44–48). Perfect. Not improved. Not sincere. Perfect, like the Father. Read that as the closing of a trap and not the opening of a project. He spends the Sermon driving the law inward and upward until it lands on a word no one in the room could survive, and he does it on purpose. The Pharisees heard "perfect" and reached for a system to manage it. The poor in spirit hear "perfect" and have nowhere to go but the King who is teaching them.

**The King who remakes the thing he demands**

So who can live this? Here is where we go wrong. We treat the Sermon as a project—a self-improvement regimen with a Galilean accent—and we set out to clean ourselves up enough to deserve the blessings. I have done it from a pulpit, preached this sermon as a to-do list and sent people home to try harder, which is just Pharisaism with better lighting. But the prophets already told us what kind of righteousness this is. "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33). "I will give you a new heart... I will remove the heart of stone" (Ezekiel 36:26). The righteousness that exceeds the Pharisees is not stricter compliance. It is a transplanted heart.

And the heart-deep righteousness is not only stricter; it is freer, lighter, lifted out of the exhausting performance the Pharisees were trapped in. "When you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you... that you may be seen by others" (Matthew 6:1–2). "When you pray, go into your room and shut the door" (Matthew 6:6). The whole middle of the Sermon is Jesus pulling righteousness out of the audience's sight and back into the secret place where only the Father sees. The Pharisee performed for the crowd and was paid in the crowd's applause, which is the only wage he would ever get. The remade heart gives and prays and fasts for an audience of One, and is free of the exhausting work of being seen. A righteousness that lives in the heart no longer needs a stage.

That is the King who is teaching. He is not handing you a standard and walking away. He is the one who came to give the new heart that alone can keep it. The Sermon on the Mount drives you to despair of your own righteousness precisely so it can drive you to his. The poor in spirit are blessed because they have stopped pretending to be rich—and the kingdom belongs to the ones who finally come empty-handed.

So you read these chapters and you feel the floor give way, and that is mercy. The blessing was never for the people who measured up. It was for the people who knew they never would, and came to the King who remakes hearts anyway.

The kingdom begins in the heart.

## Two Roads and the Day the House Comes Down
*Why hearing the King is not the same as belonging to him*

**Text:** Matthew 7:13–7:29 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 30:19 · Jeremiah 17:9–10 · Psalm 1:6 · Luke 6:46

The Sermon on the Mount does not end with reflection. It ends with a fork in the road and a house falling down. Jesus has spent three chapters describing the blessed life and the remade heart, and now he refuses to let anyone walk away thinking it was a lecture to admire. He forces a choice. Two gates. Two trees. Two confessions. Two foundations. And in every pair, only one of them lives.

**Two gates, and the popular road goes nowhere good**

"Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few" (Matthew 7:13–14). Moses had set the same choice before Israel: "I have set before you life and death... therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Jesus is not offering a spectrum of acceptable lifestyles. He is naming two destinations and telling you the crowd is on the wrong road. We were raised to trust the crowd—if everyone is doing it, it must be safe. Jesus says the crowd is precisely the evidence it is not.

**The confession that does not save**

Then comes the most frightening sentence in the chapter, and it is aimed at religious people, not pagans. "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father" (Matthew 7:21). And it gets worse. "On that day many will say to me, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name?'... And then will I declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from me'" (Matthew 7:22–23).

Read that slowly. These are not people who rejected Jesus. These are people who used his name, did ministry in his name, and were certain they were in. And the verdict is not "you fell away." It is "I never knew you." There was never a relationship. There was activity. Jeremiah saw the heart's capacity for this exact self-deception: "The heart is deceitful above all things... who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). You can fool the church. You can fool the elders. You can stand in a pulpit and fool yourself. You cannot fool the King.

**Two builders, and the storm that tells the truth**

So Jesus ends with two men building houses. They look identical—same blueprint, same skyline, both hearing the same words. The difference is invisible until the weather changes. "Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock" (Matthew 7:24). The other man "hears these words of mine and does not do them" (Matthew 7:26), and "the rain fell, and the floods came... and it fell, and great was the fall of it" (Matthew 7:27).

Notice the only difference between the two builders. It is not hearing. They both heard. It is doing. The flood does not create the weakness in the foundation. The flood reveals what was always there. Read the foolish man's mistake again, because Jesus is precise about it. "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them" (Matthew 7:26). Not everyone who rejects them. Everyone who hears and does not do. The foolish builder is a churchgoer. He is in the room for the sermon. He nods at the right lines. His failure is not absence; it is the gap between the hearing and the doing, the gap we have learned to live inside comfortably.

And here is the turn, because I have built on sand and called it rock. I have heard the word every Sunday of my adult life, taught it, preached it, and walked out of buildings where I had just exposited a text I had not obeyed in a single area of my own house. Hearing is the most spiritual-feeling way there is to disobey. You leave moved, informed, agreeing—and you have done nothing. The man who claps loudest at the sermon and changes nothing built the house that falls.

Luke records the King asking it bluntly: "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?" (Luke 6:46).

Sit in the storm a moment longer, because Jesus chose the image with care. He does not say the wise man's house never meets weather. Both houses get the same rain, the same flood, the same wind beating against the walls. The Christian life is not the absence of storms. It is a foundation that holds when they come. The grief arrives at both doors. The diagnosis comes to both men. The marriage strains and the body fails and the doubt rises in the wise builder's house too. The only question the flood answers is what the house was sitting on, and you do not get to choose that in the storm. You choose it now, on a clear day, in the quiet decision to do the word and not merely admire it.

**The authority that makes the demand and bore the storm**

The chapter closes with the crowd's reaction: "the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" (Matthew 7:28–29). The scribes quoted other rabbis. Jesus quoted no one. "I say to you." He speaks as the lawgiver, not the commentator—because he is the King.

And this is the mercy under the warning. The same King who says "depart from me" is the King who went out into the storm himself. The flood that should have fallen on the foolish builder fell on him at the cross. He stood in the weather we earned. So the call to do his words is not a call to build a righteousness that saves you—you cannot. It is a call to build your life on the only foundation that held when the floods came, the rock that is Christ himself. The Lord knows the way of the righteous (Psalm 1:6). The question this passage will not let you leave without facing is whether he knows you—or only your résumé.

Hearing is not yet obeying.

## Authority Over Everything That Breaks Us
*The King who came not for the healthy but for the sick*

**Text:** Matthew 8–9 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:4 · Hosea 6:6 · Numbers 27:17 · Ezekiel 34:5

For three chapters the King has spoken. Now he acts. Matthew gathers a sweep of miracles—nine or ten of them, stacked fast—and the cumulative effect is overwhelming on purpose. Leprosy, paralysis, fever, a storm, two demoniacs, a hemorrhage of twelve years, a dead girl, blindness, muteness. Jesus touches every category of thing that breaks a human life, and not one of them resists him. The Sermon told you the King has authority to teach. These chapters show you the authority runs all the way down.

**He touches what the law said not to touch**

The first man is a leper—the untouchable, the one the law quarantined, the one no rabbi would go near. "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" (Matthew 8:2). And Jesus does the unthinkable thing first. "Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him" (Matthew 8:3). He touches the untouchable before he heals him. Disease did not flow from the leper into Jesus. Cleanness flowed from Jesus into the leper. That is the direction the whole gospel runs.

Then authority over distance—the centurion's servant healed with a word, the centurion himself a Gentile soldier of the occupying army, whose faith makes Jesus marvel. "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith" (Matthew 8:10). The man who understands authority best is not a rabbi. It is a Roman officer who knows that a word from the one in command is enough, because he gives orders all day and watches them obeyed. He does not need Jesus to come to the house. He needs Jesus to speak. And Jesus marvels—one of only two times in the Gospels he is said to marvel at anything—because real faith had shown up in the last place Israel expected it, in a Gentile, in a uniform, outside the covenant. The kingdom was already leaking past the borders the religious had drawn around it.

Authority over the storm: "he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm" (Matthew 8:26). The men in the boat ask the question the chapters are designed to provoke: "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?" (Matthew 8:27). Authority over demons, who know exactly who he is when the religious experts do not. And Matthew tells us what is happening underneath it all: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases" (Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53:4). The miracles are not magic tricks. They are the down payment on the cross, where the bearing becomes total.

**Authority over the thing under all the others**

Then the paralytic is lowered in, and Jesus does not heal the legs first. "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven" (Matthew 9:2). The scribes are scandalized—rightly, by their own logic—because only God forgives sins. And Jesus makes the connection explicit: "Which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'?... that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (Matthew 9:5–6). The healed body is proof of the deeper authority. Paralysis is a symptom. Sin is the disease. Jesus heals the legs so you will believe him about the soul.

**The physician who came for the sick—which is the confession, not the insult**

Then the line that names the whole point. Jesus calls Matthew, a tax collector, from his booth—a collaborator, a traitor to his own people for Roman money. And he eats with him and his friends, and the Pharisees are appalled. Jesus answers, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners" (Matthew 9:12–13, quoting Hosea 6:6).

Here is where it turns on us, and the turn is sharper than we let it be. We hear "I came for sinners" as comfort, and it is—but only if you are willing to sit in the sinner's chair. The Pharisees were not appalled because they were evil. They were appalled because they thought they were well. And I know that chair. I have looked down a pew at the obvious sinner and felt the quiet satisfaction of comparison, which is the precise spiritual posture Jesus is rebuking. The physician came for the sick. If you have decided you are healthy, you have decided you do not need him—and there is no mercy in that, only the dignity of dying of a disease you refused to name.

The chapters end with Jesus looking at the crowds, "and he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" (Matthew 9:36). The word reaches all the way back to Moses praying that Israel not be "as sheep that have no shepherd" (Numbers 27:17), and to Ezekiel's indictment of the shepherds who fed themselves and let the flock scatter (Ezekiel 34:5). The crowds did not need a better program. They needed a shepherd. And the shepherd had come, looking at the harassed and the helpless, which is to say looking at us.

And notice what compassion moves him to do—not a program, not a campaign, but a prayer and a sending. "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest" (Matthew 9:37–38). The physician who came for the sick looks at a sea of harassed people and does not despair and does not strategize. He grieves, and he sends. The same authority that calmed the storm and forgave the paralytic and touched the leper is now reaching for ordinary people to carry it into the next town. He came for the sick. And then he turned the healed into the ones he sends to the still-sick, which is the only way the harvest was ever going to be brought in.

He came for the sick.

## Sheep Among Wolves and the Cost of Carrying His Name
*What it actually costs to be sent by the King*

**Text:** Matthew 10 · **Supporting:** Micah 7:6 · Isaiah 53:3 · 2 Timothy 3:12 · Matthew 16:25

Jesus has just looked at the harassed crowds and called them sheep without a shepherd. You expect him to comfort them. Instead he turns to the twelve and sends them out as shepherds-in-training, and the commission he gives them is the most honest job description in the Bible. He does not recruit with promises of success. He recruits with a warning. "Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves" (Matthew 10:16). Read that again as the strategy it is. He sends sheep at wolves. On purpose.

**The mission is an extension of his own**

First, what he gives them. "He gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction" (Matthew 10:1). The very things we watched him do in chapters eight and nine, he now hands to the twelve. "Proclaim as you go, saying, 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons" (Matthew 10:7–8). The mission is not the disciples' idea. It is his ministry, extended through their hands. They go with his message and his power, not their own.

And it is, for now, to Israel: "Go nowhere among the Gentiles... but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matthew 10:5–6). The shepherd goes first to the flock that was promised the covenant. The nations come later, and they come because of a cross and an empty tomb that have not happened yet.

Then Jesus tells them how to travel, and the instructions are stranger than we admit. "Acquire no gold nor silver nor copper for your belts, no bag for your journey, nor two tunics nor sandals nor a staff" (Matthew 10:9–10). Go out with nothing. No reserves, no backup plan, no insurance against the trip going badly. We would call that irresponsible. Jesus calls it the posture of a man who actually believes the kingdom he is announcing. The empty bag is the sermon. A messenger who has packed for every contingency does not look like someone who trusts the King who sent him. He looks like a man hedging his bets. The mission goes out exposed on purpose, so that the power on display is never confused with the resources of the men carrying it.

**The cost is not exaggerated**

Then the King stops promising power and starts naming the price, and he does not soften it. "You will be hated by all for my name's sake" (Matthew 10:22). "Brother will deliver brother over to death" (Matthew 10:21). He quotes the prophet Micah, who saw a society so corrupt that "a man's enemies are the men of his own house" (Micah 7:6; Matthew 10:36). The gospel will divide kitchens. "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword" (Matthew 10:34). He is not describing a failure of the mission. He is describing the mission working—the light exposing the dark, and the dark hating it.

And then the demand that makes modern Christianity flinch. "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:37). "And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:38). The cross was not yet a symbol on a wall. It was a Roman execution device, and everyone hearing him knew what it meant: a man carrying a cross was a dead man on his way to die. He is telling his followers to count themselves dead already. "A disciple is not above his teacher" (Matthew 10:24). They mocked him as "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3); his servants should expect no parade.

**The losing that is finding, and the fear that is misplaced**

Now turn it on yourself, because we have built a version of following Jesus he would not recognize—a faith that costs a Sunday morning and an occasional awkward conversation and nothing else. I have preached a discipleship that fit comfortably inside a respectable middle-class life, which is to say I have preached the half of this chapter that recruits and skipped the half that warns. Paul did not flinch from it: "all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted" (2 Timothy 3:12). We have made that verse optional. Jesus made it a guarantee.

But here is the mercy buried in the cost. "Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 10:39). The losing is not the tragedy. The losing is the way in. The man who clutches his life—his comfort, his reputation, his family's approval, his safety—will watch it slip through his fingers anyway, because nothing held that tightly survives. The one who lays it down for Christ discovers it was never lost; it was given back, larger, his. And the fear is relocated, not removed: "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28). The wolves can take your life. They cannot take you.

And there is a second mercy, larger than your safety. "So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 10:32). The confession that costs you your family's approval here is the confession the Son carries up to the Father's throne and speaks over you there. What looks like loss at the kitchen table is being recorded in heaven as the Son owning you before God. That is the trade the chapter is asking you to make—a name lost among men for a name spoken by Christ before the Father. Stated that way, the cost stops looking like sacrifice and starts looking like the best exchange a person could make.

The same King who sends sheep among wolves says, "even the hairs of your head are all numbered" (Matthew 10:30). He does not promise you will be spared. He promises you will be counted. He sends you into a cost he has already measured to the cent—and he sends you as one who walked it first, all the way to the cross he tells you to carry.

Following him will cost you.

## Come to Me, All Who Are Weary
*The King hidden from the wise, given to the worn-out*

**Text:** Matthew 11–12 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 42:1–3 · Jeremiah 6:16 · Isaiah 6:9–10 · Hosea 6:6

Even John the Baptist doubts. The man who baptized Jesus, who heard the voice from heaven, sends word from a prison cell: "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" (Matthew 11:3). This is the giant of the prophets, and he is not sure. Matthew puts John's doubt at the front of these chapters so we will not be surprised by all the rejection that follows—and so we will see that Jesus does not crush the bruised reed when it bends.

**The cities that watched the miracles and yawned**

Jesus answers John gently—"the blind receive their sight... and the poor have good news preached to them" (Matthew 11:5)—and then turns to the cities that saw all of it and repented of nothing. "Woe to you, Chorazin... Bethsaida... Capernaum" (Matthew 11:21–23). These were not pagan cities. These were the towns where most of his miracles were done. They had front-row seats. And Jesus says Sodom would have repented if it had seen what they saw. The most dangerous place to stand is not far from Jesus. It is near him, comfortable, unmoved.

Then the explanation, and it is staggering. "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children" (Matthew 11:25). The kingdom is not hidden from sinners. It is hidden from the wise—from the experts, the credentialed, the ones too sophisticated to come empty. It is given to children, to the weary, to people with nothing to bring. This is the same scandal running through the whole Gospel: the kingdom goes to the bankrupt and bypasses the impressive.

**The invitation in the middle of all the rejection**

And right there, surrounded by doubt and woe and hardening, comes the most tender sentence Jesus ever spoke. "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:28–29). Jeremiah had pleaded with Israel: "ask for the ancient paths... and find rest for your souls" (Jeremiah 6:16). Israel answered, "We will not walk in it." Now the rest itself stands in front of them and says, come.

Notice who is invited. The weary. The heavy-laden. Not the rested, not the strong, not the ones who have it together. The qualification for coming to Christ is exhaustion. If you are tired of carrying yourself, you are exactly the person he is talking to. And the yoke is not no burden—it is his burden, easy because he pulls beside you, against the religion of the Pharisees that piled weight on people and lifted not a finger to help.

And weigh the words he uses to describe himself, because they are the only place in the Gospels where Jesus tells us what is in his own heart. "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29). Not stern. Not exhausting. Not impossible to please. Of all the things he could have said about himself—I am holy, I am mighty, I am the judge of the living and the dead, every one of them true—the self-description he hands the weary is gentle and lowly. This matters because the reason most people will not come is that they have imagined a Christ who is disappointed in them, arms crossed, waiting for them to clean up before they approach. He says the opposite about himself in his own words. The one who runs the universe is, toward the heavy-laden, gentle. Lowly. The exact opposite of what your shame expects.

**The line you cannot cross back over—and why it is not for the weary**

Then chapter twelve darkens hard. Jesus heals on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees, watching mercy with their own eyes, conspire to destroy him. He casts out a demon, and they say he does it "by Beelzebul, the prince of demons" (Matthew 12:24). They look at the undeniable work of God and call it the work of Satan. And Jesus names a sin with no forgiveness: "blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" (Matthew 12:31).

This terrifies tender people, and it should not. Look at who commits it. Not the doubter—John doubted and Jesus comforted him. Not the weary—they are invited by name. The unforgivable hardness belongs to people who see the Spirit's work clearly and deliberately, knowingly, call it demonic to protect their own position. Isaiah saw this judicial hardening: a people who "keep on hearing, but do not understand" until their own hearts are calloused shut (Isaiah 6:9–10). It is not a sin you stumble into. It is a fortress you build, brick by brick, against the obvious.

And here is where I have to stop pointing at the Pharisees and look in the mirror, because I have called my own hardness discernment. I have watched God work in someone I had already written off and looked for a reason to discount it, which is the Pharisees' move in a smaller key. The opposite of that hardness is not cleverness. It is the weariness that finally comes with empty hands. The Father desires "mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matthew 12:7, quoting Hosea 6:6)—and mercy is precisely what the hard heart cannot receive, because to receive mercy you must first admit you need it.

So the two paths in these chapters could not be further apart. One hardens against the light until the door it slams stays shut. The other is too tired to pretend any longer and finally comes. The bruised reed he will not break; the smoldering wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3). He came for the worn-out. The only question is whether you are done carrying yourself.

Come, all who are weary.

## The Kingdom That Looks Like Almost Nothing
*Why the reign of God comes hidden before it comes in glory*

**Text:** Matthew 13 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 6:9–10 · Daniel 2:34–35 · Psalm 78:2 · Ezekiel 17:23

When Jesus finally explains how the kingdom works, he does not give a strategy. He tells stories about dirt, weeds, seeds, yeast, buried treasure, and a fishing net. Seven parables, and every one of them is correcting the same wrong assumption. The crowd expected the kingdom to arrive like an army—visible, immediate, overwhelming, all enemies destroyed by Tuesday. Jesus says it comes like a seed. Small. Hidden. Contested. Slow. And only at the very end does it become what everyone was waiting for.

**The same word, four different soils**

The first parable sets up all the rest. A sower scatters seed, and it lands on four soils. The path, where birds snatch it. Rocky ground, where it springs up fast and dies in the sun. Thorns, where "the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word" (Matthew 13:22). And good soil, which "bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold" (Matthew 13:23).

Notice what is constant. The seed is the same. The sower is the same. The word of the kingdom goes out identically to all four. The difference is entirely the soil—the heart that receives it. We want to make the failure the preacher's fault, or the seed's, or the times we live in. Jesus locates it in the ground. The same sermon hardens one heart and saves another, and the variable is not the sermon.

And Jesus tells us why he teaches in parables, quoting the most uncomfortable text in Isaiah: "You will indeed hear but never understand... For this people's heart has grown dull" (Matthew 13:14–15, from Isaiah 6:9–10). The parables both reveal and conceal. They open the kingdom to the hungry and close it to the dull, which is its own kind of mercy and its own kind of judgment, and the difference between them is the soil.

Linger on the thorny ground, because it is the soil that catches respectable people. The seed on the path never started. The seed on the rock died fast and obviously. But the thorny ground grows the plant—it looks alive for a long time—"and the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful" (Matthew 13:22). This is the soil that does not look like rebellion. It looks like a busy, prosperous, churchgoing life that quietly has no fruit, strangled not by hatred of God but by the slow, respectable weeds of worry and wealth and a hundred good things crowding out the one. No one decides to be thorny ground. You become it the way a garden becomes a thicket—by neglect, one undealt-with care at a time.

**The kingdom grows where you cannot see it work**

Then the parables of smallness. The mustard seed, "the smallest of all seeds," becomes a tree where the birds nest (Matthew 13:31–32)—Ezekiel's image of God planting a sprig that grows into a noble cedar (Ezekiel 17:23). The leaven a woman hides in the flour until all of it is leavened (Matthew 13:33). The kingdom does not announce itself with trumpets. It works the way yeast works—invisibly, from the inside, until one day the whole loaf has risen and you cannot find the moment it changed.

And the wheat and the weeds. An enemy sows weeds among the wheat, and the servants want to rip them out now. The master says no—"lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest" (Matthew 13:29–30). Here is the patience that drives zealous people crazy. The kingdom comes into a field that still has weeds in it. The church is mixed. The world is mixed. And the sorting is not your job and not now. "The harvest is the end of the age" (Matthew 13:39).

**The treasure worth everything, and the King who is the field**

Then two short parables that name the kingdom's worth. A man finds treasure hidden in a field and "in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field" (Matthew 13:44). A merchant finds one pearl and sells everything for it (Matthew 13:45–46). The accent is on the joy. He does not sell everything grimly, as a sacrifice. He sells everything gladly, because he has seen what he is getting. The kingdom costs you everything and is worth more than everything, and the man who understands that is not making a sacrifice. He is making the best deal of his life.

Now turn it on us. We want a kingdom we can see—a Christianity that wins visibly, that fixes the culture by Friday, that vindicates us in front of the people who mocked us. And when the kingdom comes hidden instead—small, slow, mixed, contested—we are tempted to think it failed, or to grab the sword and start pulling weeds ourselves. I have done the weeding. I have stood in a pulpit ready to sort the field God told me to leave alone, certain I could tell wheat from weed at a glance, which is exactly the arrogance the master forbids. The faith that demands the harvest now does not trust the sower.

But the seed that looks like nothing is the same seed Daniel saw—a stone cut from a mountain by no human hand, that struck the empires and grew "a great mountain and filled the whole earth" (Daniel 2:35). The mustard seed wins. The leaven leavens the whole loaf. The hidden treasure is real treasure. And the field you are asked to buy with everything has the King himself buried in it, the one who told these things "to utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world" (Matthew 13:35, quoting Psalm 78:2). He came small the first time. He will not come small the second.

The kingdom grows hidden, then revealed.

## You Are the Christ—and the Cross
*The confession Jesus blessed and then redefined*

**Text:** Matthew 16:13–16:28 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:3–6 · Daniel 7:13–14 · Psalm 49:7–8 · Mark 8:33

Everything in Matthew has been building to this one conversation outside the city of Caesarea Philippi. Jesus has healed and taught and fed thousands, and the crowds still cannot say who he is. So he asks the question directly. "Who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). And Peter, for one shining moment, gets it exactly right—and then, within six verses, gets it so wrong that Jesus calls him Satan. Both things are true. That is the heart of this passage, and the heart of the gospel.

**The confession that heaven gave him**

"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). It is the high point of the Gospel so far. The Christ—the anointed King, the one David's line was promised. The Son of the living God—not a prophet, not a teacher, but God's own Son. And Jesus blesses it without reservation. "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah. For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 16:17). Peter did not reason his way here. The Father opened his eyes. No one confesses Christ truly except by revelation, which means the confession in your own mouth, if it is real, is itself a gift you did not generate.

And on this confession Jesus builds: "on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18). The church is not built on Peter's strength—we are about to watch that strength collapse. It is built on the confessed truth of who Jesus is. Hell has been throwing itself at that rock for two thousand years and has not moved it.

**The redefinition that broke Peter's idea of the Messiah**

Then, immediately—Matthew says "from that time"—Jesus pours content into the title Peter just used, and the content is a horror. "He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things... and be killed, and on the third day be raised" (Matthew 16:21). The Christ. Killed. Peter cannot bear it. He takes Jesus aside and rebukes him—rebukes the Son of God—"Far be it from you, Lord. This shall never happen to you" (Matthew 16:22).

And Jesus turns and says the hardest words he ever spoke to a friend: "Get behind me, Satan. You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man" (Matthew 16:23). Six verses from "blessed are you" to "Satan." What changed? Peter wanted a Christ without a cross. A King who conquers but does not die. A Messiah who fixes the Romans and skips Golgotha. And Jesus names that desire for exactly what it is—the same temptation the devil offered in the wilderness, the kingdoms without the cross. Peter meant it as love. Jesus heard it as the enemy.

Stay on that moment, because it is the most important hinge in Matthew, and the cost lands first on the One who absorbs the rebuke. The same Peter, in the same breath of revelation, is the door the old temptation walks back through. The wilderness offered Jesus the kingdoms without the cross. Now a friend offers him the same thing, dressed as concern, dressed as love. And Jesus does not soften the answer because the source is dear to him. He turns and names it Satan, not because Peter is wicked, but because a cross-less Christ is the one lie that would damn the whole world, and it is being whispered to him by the man he just called the rock. He will go to the cross over the objection of his closest friend, alone in the rightness of it.

Here is what we keep missing. Peter's mistake is not believing too little about Jesus. It is the right title attached to the wrong story. "Christ" was correct. "Crucified Christ" was unthinkable. But the prophets had already drawn the suffering King—"he was pierced for our transgressions... and with his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). No man could pay this ransom; "the ransom of their life is costly" (Psalm 49:7–8). Only the Son of Man whom Daniel saw, given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14), could go down into death and come up with the keys.

**The cross is not a detour to the throne—it is the throne**

So why does this matter for us, not just for Peter? Because we are all Peter. We want the Christ who blesses the life we have planned and stays off the cross-shaped parts of it. And then Jesus extends the redefinition from himself to us: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:24–25).

This is the part I preach to others more easily than I live. I have wanted a discipleship that costs my opinions but not my comfort, a following of Jesus that looks like the King's glory and never like his suffering, which is to say I have wanted Peter's Messiah and called it faith. A cross-less Christ produces a cross-less Christian, and a cross-less Christian has missed the entire shape of the thing. "What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?" (Matthew 16:26). The world Peter wanted to save Jesus from was the world that could not be saved any other way.

The mercy is that the One who tells you to take up your cross took up his first, and carried it for you, and came out of the tomb on the third day exactly as he said. The crucified Christ is the risen Christ. The throne was always shaped like a cross. And the confession that saves you is not just "you are the Christ." It is "you are the crucified Christ"—and I will follow you there.

The Christ is a crucified Christ.

## Greatness That Looks Like a Child and Forgiveness With No Floor
*How the King orders the life of his church*

**Text:** Matthew 18 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 34:11–16 · Colossians 3:13 · Ephesians 4:32 · Leviticus 19:17

The disciples ask the wrong question, and Jesus uses it to reorder everything. "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" (Matthew 18:1). They are already jockeying for rank in a kingdom that has not arrived, already building a hierarchy, already certain greatness means being above someone. And Jesus answers by calling over a child—the lowest-status person in that world, with no power, no standing, nothing to negotiate with—and stands the child in the middle of them. This is what the whole chapter does. It takes every instinct we have about greatness, pursuit, conflict, and mercy, and turns it upside down.

**Greatness is downward**

"Unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest" (Matthew 18:3–4). Greatness in the kingdom is not climbing. It is descending. The child has no résumé, no standing, no claim—and that is the qualification, not the obstacle. Then Jesus turns fierce about how the lowly are treated: "whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matthew 18:6). The King who welcomes the small will not tolerate the strong despising them.

**The shepherd who leaves ninety-nine for one**

Then the lost sheep. A man has a hundred sheep and one wanders off. "Does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?" (Matthew 18:12). And "it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish" (Matthew 18:14). This is Ezekiel's God made flesh—"I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed" (Ezekiel 34:11–16). The kingdom does not write off the straying one as acceptable loss. It goes after the one. We do the math the other way: ninety-nine is a good retention rate, cut the loss. Heaven leaves the ninety-nine on the mountain and goes out into the dark for the one.

And notice the order of the chapter, because it is not random. Jesus puts the childlike lowliness first, then the relentless pursuit of the straying, then honest confrontation, and only then the unlimited forgiveness—and he frames all of it around the little ones the strong are tempted to despise. The whole architecture is built to protect the weak from the powerful inside the church. The same community that pursues the wandering sheep is the community that confronts sin honestly and forgives without ceiling, because all three are the same posture aimed at the same person: do not lose the one. Most of our church conflicts come from doing one of these without the others—confrontation without pursuit becomes cruelty, pursuit without confrontation becomes enabling, and forgiveness without either becomes a doormat. Jesus refuses to let us pick one. He hands us all three and calls it love.

And then, because the church will have sin in it, Jesus gives the only process he ever laid out for confronting it. Go to your brother privately first (Matthew 18:15). Not to others first. To him. Take one or two if he will not listen. Tell the church only as a last resort. The whole movement aims at one word: "if he listens to you, you have gained your brother" (Matthew 18:15). The goal of confrontation is not winning. It is gaining. Leviticus already commanded it: "you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him" (Leviticus 19:17). Honest confrontation is itself a form of love. Silence in the face of a brother's sin is not kindness. It is abandonment with good manners.

**Forgiveness with no ceiling—because yours had none**

Then Peter, trying to be generous, asks how many times he must forgive. "As many as seven times?" (Matthew 18:21)—already triple the rabbinic standard. Jesus answers, "seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:22), which is to say, stop counting. And he tells the parable that explains why. A servant owes the king ten thousand talents—an unpayable, absurd debt, the wages of more lifetimes than anyone has. The king forgives all of it. And that same servant walks out and seizes a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii—a few months' wages, real money, but nothing against what he was just forgiven—and throws him in prison (Matthew 18:23–30).

The king's verdict is the chapter's verdict: "should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:33). Here is where it stops being about other people. I have nursed a grudge over a hundred denarii while standing forgiven of ten thousand talents. I have stood in a pulpit and preached grace on Sunday and rehearsed someone's offense against me on Monday, which is the unforgiving servant in a clerical collar. The math of the parable is brutal and exact. The debt you forgive is always the hundred denarii. The debt you were forgiven is always the ten thousand talents. And the man who cannot forgive the small thing has not yet understood the size of the large thing.

Paul says it plainly: "forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" (Colossians 3:13)—"as God in Christ forgave you" (Ephesians 4:32). Notice the order. Not forgive in order to be forgiven. Forgive because you were. The unpayable debt was canceled at the cross, where the King himself absorbed the cost the servant could never cover. And a heart that has truly stood in that flood of mercy cannot turn around and choke a brother over pocket change. If it does, the parable asks a question that should keep us up at night: did that heart ever really understand it was forgiven at all?

Forgive as you were forgiven.

## The Last Made First and the Ransom That Bought Them
*The King overturns the world's accounting on the road to Jerusalem*

**Text:** Matthew 19–20 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:10–11 · Genesis 2:24 · Psalm 49:6–9 · Philippians 2:5–8

Jesus is walking toward Jerusalem to die, and on the way he dismantles every scorecard we keep. Marriage, children, money, reward, rank—one by one he takes the things we use to measure who is winning and turns them over. The disciples keep doing the math the world taught them. Jesus keeps showing them the kingdom runs on a different ledger entirely, and the ledger ends at a cross where the King pays a debt that was not his.

**The rich man who could not let go**

A young man runs up—decent, sincere, religious—and asks, "what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" (Matthew 19:16). He has kept the commandments since boyhood, and he means it. And Jesus, loving him, names the one thing he is holding onto. "Go, sell what you possess and give to the poor... and come, follow me" (Matthew 19:21). "When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Matthew 19:22).

He did not walk away because the price was too high in dollars. He walked away because his money owned him and he could not bear to be free of it. "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God" (Matthew 19:24). The disciples are stunned—"who then can be saved?" (Matthew 19:25)—because in their world wealth was the sign of God's favor. Jesus answers, "with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (Matthew 19:26). No one buys their way in. The psalmist said it long ago—no man can ransom his own soul, "for the ransom of their life is costly" (Psalm 49:7–8). The rich young man's tragedy is that he came to purchase what could only be received, and he could not put down his purse long enough to open his hands.

And do not miss that Jesus loved him while naming the one thing he could not give up. This is not a man who failed a personality test. He was sincere, moral, and earnest, and Jesus, looking at him, loved him—and still would not lower the price, because the price was the very thing strangling him. The kindest thing Jesus could do for a man owned by his money was to ask for the money. We read it as harsh. It was the only honest love available. A teacher who let the rich man keep both his wealth and his illusion of discipleship would have loved him less, not more. The hard word was the loving word, and the man walked away sorrowful because, for once, someone had refused to flatter him.

**The wage that grace refuses to make fair**

Then Peter, who did leave everything, asks the natural follow-up: "what then will we have?" (Matthew 19:27). And Jesus answers with a parable designed to offend our sense of fairness. A master hires workers at dawn, and more at nine, at noon, at three, and at five in the afternoon. At the end of the day he pays them all the same—a full denarius, even the ones who worked one hour. The dawn workers are furious. "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day" (Matthew 20:12).

And the master's answer is the gospel: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:15). Here is what offends us, and we should let it. We want grace to be fair, which means we want to be paid more than the latecomer because we put in more hours. But grace is not wages. Grace is gift. And the moment you start calculating what your years of service have earned you, you have left the kingdom and gone back to the marketplace. I know that arithmetic. I have stood in a pulpit with two decades of ministry behind me and felt, somewhere underneath, that I had earned a better place in line than the man saved last Tuesday—which is the dawn worker's grumble in a robe. "The last will be first, and the first last" (Matthew 20:16). Grace humbles the one who thinks he earned it as much as it lifts the one who knows she did not.

**Greatness is a ransom, and the King paid it himself**

Then the mother of James and John asks for thrones—one son at his right hand, one at his left (Matthew 20:21). The other ten are indignant, which means they wanted the same thing and were just slower to ask. And Jesus gathers them and overturns the last scorecard. "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them... It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:25–26).

And then the sentence the whole two chapters were built to reach: "even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). There it is. The King defines greatness, and then he goes and embodies it on a cross. He is walking to Jerusalem as he says this, walking toward the place where the serving becomes dying. Isaiah saw it—"when his soul makes an offering for guilt... the righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous" (Isaiah 53:10–11). Paul saw it—the One who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant... and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:7–8).

The rich man could not pay the ransom. The dawn workers tried to earn it. The disciples wanted thrones above it. And the King simply paid it—his own life, given for many, the price no one else could cover. That is the accounting of the kingdom. The first who insist on being first will find themselves last, still clutching a denarius they thought they earned. And the last, who came with nothing, will find themselves first, holding a gift bought with blood.

The first will be last.

## The King Enters and Indicts His Own House
*Judgment that begins not with the pagans but with the temple*

**Text:** Matthew 21–23 · **Supporting:** Zechariah 9:9 · Isaiah 56:7 · Jeremiah 7:11 · Hosea 9:10

The King finally comes to his capital, and he does not come on a war horse. He comes on a donkey. "Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey" (Matthew 21:5, quoting Zechariah 9:9). The crowds spread their cloaks and shout Hosanna, expecting a conqueror who will throw out the Romans. They have the right King and the wrong kingdom. And the first thing this humble King does when he reaches the city is not strike Rome. It is walk into the temple and overturn the tables. Judgment, when it comes, does not start with the enemies outside. It starts inside the house of God.

**The house of prayer turned into a market**

"My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers" (Matthew 21:13). He is quoting two prophets at once—Isaiah's vision of a temple open to all nations as a house of prayer (Isaiah 56:7), and Jeremiah's furious charge that the people had turned the temple into a robbers' hideout, a place to feel safe while doing evil everywhere else (Jeremiah 7:11). The temple had become a religious operation with the religion drained out. The forms were immaculate. The God was gone.

Then the fig tree. Jesus, hungry, comes to a fig tree full of leaves and finds no fruit, and he curses it, and it withers (Matthew 21:18–19). This is not a tantrum about breakfast. It is a parable in an action. The tree had everything that advertised fruit—every leaf in place—and produced nothing. So did the temple. So did the leaders. So does a religion of show. Hosea had grieved over Israel the same way: "Like the first fruit on the fig tree... I saw your fathers" (Hosea 9:10)—promise that came to nothing. The leaves were lush. The branches were bare.

And this is the danger that lives in a religion of leaves. Leaves are easy. Leaves are what you grow when you want to look fruitful without the slow, costly work of bearing actual fruit. Attendance is leaves. Right answers are leaves. A reputation for godliness is leaves. The temple had all of it—the crowds, the sacrifices, the schedule of feasts running like clockwork—and the King walked up hungry and found nothing to eat. That is the most frightening sentence in these chapters for anyone whose life is full of religious activity. You can be covered in leaves and have no figs, and the only one who can tell the difference is the King who comes looking for fruit, not foliage.

**The tenants who killed the heir**

Then Jesus tells the parable that explains why he is doing all of this. A master plants a vineyard and rents it to tenants and goes away. He sends servants for the fruit, and the tenants beat them and kill them. Finally he sends his son—"They will respect my son" (Matthew 21:37). And the tenants say, "This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance" (Matthew 21:38). And they throw him out of the vineyard and kill him.

The leaders understood it perfectly. "They perceived that he was speaking about them" (Matthew 21:45). God planted Israel as a vineyard, sent prophet after prophet who were beaten and killed, and finally sent his Son—and the Son was standing in front of them telling them they were about to murder him. And here is what should stop every religious professional cold: the tenants did not kill the heir out of unbelief. They killed him precisely because they knew who he was. "This is the heir." They recognized the Son and murdered him anyway, because his arrival threatened their claim on the vineyard. That is the most dangerous form of unbelief there is—not ignorance of Christ, but accurate knowledge of him resented because he comes to take back what we have decided is ours. The chief priests knew their Bibles. That is what makes the parable a warning to the people who know their Bibles best. "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (Matthew 21:42). The judgment is not arbitrary. It falls on tenants who killed every messenger and were about to kill the Heir.

**The seven woes—and the mirror they hold up**

Then chapter twenty-three, the most withering thing Jesus ever said, seven times over: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites" (Matthew 23:13–29). And read what he actually condemns, because it is uncomfortably close to home. They tithe their herb gardens and neglect "justice and mercy and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23). They clean the outside of the cup while inside it is full of greed (Matthew 23:25). They are "like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones" (Matthew 23:27). The indictment is never that they did too much religion. It is that the religion was a surface over a corpse.

And here is where I cannot stand at a safe distance, because I wear the title these men wore. I am a religious professional. I tithe and study and stand up front, and the temptation Jesus names—to polish the visible and neglect the heart, to perform a righteousness for the crowd while something rots underneath—is not the Pharisees' temptation. It is mine, every week. The whitewashed tomb is the occupational hazard of anyone who gets paid to be good in public. If I read Matthew 23 and feel only satisfaction at those ancient hypocrites getting what they deserved, I have proven I am one of them.

And yet listen to how the woes end. Not in rage. In tears. "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not" (Matthew 23:37). The King who indicts his house is weeping over it. The judgment is grief, not vengeance. He is not an enemy come to destroy the temple. He is the Son the tenants are about to kill, looking at the city that will kill him, longing to gather them—and refused. The cornerstone they reject is the only foundation that would have held.

The King judges his own house.

## Stay Awake, for the Master Is Coming
*What the King commands of servants who do not know the hour*

**Text:** Matthew 24–25 · **Supporting:** Daniel 7:13–14 · Amos 5:18–20 · 1 Thessalonians 5:2–6 · Proverbs 6:9–11

The disciples point at the temple—massive, gleaming, the center of their world—and Jesus says, "there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down" (Matthew 24:2). The thing they were sure would last forever is coming down. And on the Mount of Olives, looking across at that doomed temple, Jesus delivers his last great teaching before the cross: a long answer about the end of the age and his own return, and it lands on a single command repeated until you cannot miss it. Watch. Stay awake. Be ready. You do not know the hour.

**The day no one can schedule**

The disciples want a timetable. "What will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" (Matthew 24:3). Jesus gives them signs—wars, famines, false messiahs, persecution, the gospel preached to all nations—but he refuses the one thing they want, the date. "Concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only" (Matthew 24:36). He compares it to the days of Noah, when people "were eating and drinking... and they were unaware until the flood came" (Matthew 24:38–39). The point is not that they were wicked. The point is that they were unprepared. Normal life, right up until the door shut.

Daniel had seen the coming One: "behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man... and to him was given dominion" (Daniel 7:13–14). That King is coming back to claim the dominion. Paul says he comes "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2)—not to frighten the children of light, but to wake the ones who are asleep. "So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober" (1 Thessalonians 5:6).

**Three parables, one demand: be found ready**

So Jesus tells three stories, and each one is about being ready when readiness is no longer possible. Ten virgins wait for the bridegroom. Five bring extra oil; five do not. The bridegroom is delayed—he always is, in these parables—and comes at midnight, and the five without oil run to buy more and return to a shut door. "Lord, lord, open to us." "Truly, I say to you, I do not know you" (Matthew 25:11–12). The oil cannot be borrowed at the last minute. Some preparation is not transferable. You cannot run on someone else's faith when the bridegroom comes.

Then the talents. A master entrusts his servants with money and leaves. Two invest and double it. The third, afraid, buries his in the ground and gives it back untouched—"I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground" (Matthew 25:25). And the master is severe with him, not because he lost money, but because he risked nothing, did nothing, treated the gift as something to protect rather than to use. "You wicked and slothful servant" (Matthew 25:26). Faithfulness is not keeping your head down until the King returns. It is putting to work everything he gave you.

And notice the lie the third servant tells himself about the master. "I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow" (Matthew 25:24). His fear was downstream of a wrong picture of the one he served. He thought the master was harsh, so he played it safe, so he did nothing, so he lost everything. The servants who invested were not braver by temperament. They simply trusted the master enough to risk his money on his behalf. This is the quiet engine under all spiritual laziness—a buried suspicion that God is hard, stingy, waiting to catch us out, so we bury what he gave us and call our timidity reverence. The man who thinks God is a miser will never invest a thing. And then he will blame God for the emptiness of his own hands.

Then the sheep and the goats. The King separates the nations, and the dividing line is startling. "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink... I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). The righteous are surprised—when did we see you? "As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). Readiness, it turns out, is not abstract. It looks like bread handed to the hungry and a door opened to the stranger, done not for reward but because that is what a heart awake to the King simply does.

**The sleep I keep mistaking for peace**

Now turn it on us, because these parables are not finally about the foolish virgins or the lazy servant. They are about me. I bury talents and call it prudence. I doze through ordinary weeks and call the spiritual flatness peace. The wisdom literature already named the self-deception: "a little sleep, a little slumber... and poverty will come upon you like a robber" (Proverbs 6:10–11). Amos warned the people who longed for the day of the Lord without being ready for it—"Why would you have the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light" (Amos 5:18). The same coming is hope for the awake and terror for the asleep, and the difference is not how much you knew but whether you lived ready.

Here is the mercy in the warning. The Master who is coming is the same King who is going to the cross at the end of this very week, who will die as a ransom and rise with all authority. He does not warn us as a stranger. He warns us as the bridegroom who actually intends to come for his bride, as a master who entrusted real gifts to real servants because he means to come back and find the house alive. The shut door in the parable is grief, not glee. He does not want anyone to hear "I do not know you." He tells us now, plainly, while the oil can still be bought and the talents still invested and the hungry still fed, so that the day of his coming will be the day we have been waiting for, not the day that catches us asleep.

Stay awake. He is coming.

## The Crucified King Who Holds All Authority
*Death, an empty tomb, and a commission to the ends of the earth*

**Text:** Matthew 26–28 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:5–12 · Psalm 22:1 · Daniel 7:14 · Exodus 26:31–33

The whole Gospel has been driving here. The King who was born as Immanuel, tested in the wilderness, confessed by Peter, who entered Jerusalem on a donkey and wept over it—now he is betrayed, abandoned, condemned, and nailed to a Roman cross. And Matthew tells it without flinching, because the cross is not the failure of the kingdom. It is the coronation. The crown was always thorns. The throne was always a cross. And on the third day, the grave could not keep the King.

**Abandoned, so that we would not be**

Watch how alone he becomes. Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver. In Gethsemane he prays, "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will" (Matthew 26:39)—and his closest friends fall asleep three times while he sweats it out. Peter, who swore he would die first, denies him three times before the rooster crows and goes out and weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:75). They condemn him on false witness. They spit on him. And on the cross, in the deepest darkness, he cries the opening line of Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

That cry is the center of everything. The Son who heard "this is my beloved" at the Jordan now hears nothing but silence from heaven. Why? Because the wrath we earned was falling on him. Isaiah had written it seven hundred years before: "he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities... and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:5–6). He was forsaken so that we never will be. The abandonment was ours; he took it.

**The curtain torn from top to bottom**

Then, at the moment he dies, Matthew records something easy to read past. "And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matthew 27:51). That curtain had hung in the temple since Moses—a thick veil separating the Holy of Holies, the place of God's presence, from everyone else (Exodus 26:31–33). Only the high priest entered, once a year, with blood, trembling. The curtain said: keep out. God is holy and you are not.

And at the cross it tears. Not from the bottom, where a man might cut it. From the top, where only God could. The veil that kept sinners out of God's presence is ripped open the instant the King dies, because the death of the King is the price that opens the door. The way to God is no longer barred. It runs straight through a torn curtain and a broken body. Isaiah saw the result: "he shall see his offspring... he makes many to be accounted righteous" (Isaiah 53:10–11).

Hold the two cries side by side, because together they are the gospel. On the cross, the Son cries, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—the door of heaven closed against him. In the temple, the curtain rips top to bottom—the door of heaven opened to us. Those two things happen at the same moment, and they are the same transaction. The door slammed on the Son is the door flung open for sinners. He was shut out so we could be let in. The forsakenness was the cost of the access. Every time a guilty person now comes to God without fear, they walk through a curtain that was torn by the very abandonment the Son endured in the dark.

**All authority—and the promise that ends the book**

Then the third day. The women come to the tomb in grief and find it empty, and an angel says the sentence that splits history: "He is not here, for he has risen, as he said" (Matthew 28:6). As he said. He told them in chapter sixteen. They could not hear it then. Now the stone is rolled away, and the crucified King is the living King.

And he gathers the eleven on a mountain—the disciples who fled, who slept, who denied—and he does not rebuke them. He commissions them. "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (Matthew 28:18). This is Daniel's vision come true: "to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" (Daniel 7:14). The donkey-riding King now holds everything. And he sends his failures out as his ambassadors: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them... teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you" (Matthew 28:19–20).

Here is where it lands on us, and the landing is the whole point. We read the disciples' failures—the sleeping, the denying, the fleeing—as their shame, and we keep our own at a careful distance. We should not. I have slept in my Gethsemanes and denied him in smaller rooms than a high priest's courtyard, and the men Jesus sends to disciple the nations are precisely the men who abandoned him three days earlier. He does not commission the worthy. There are no worthy. He commissions the forgiven. The mission of the church has always been carried by people who failed the King and were sent anyway.

And the very last words of the Gospel are not a strategy or a warning. They are a presence. "And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). The book opened with a name—Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23)—and it closes by making the name a promise that does not expire. He came to be with us. He died forsaken so we would never be. He rose with all authority. And now he goes out with us, into every nation, to the end of the age, and he does not leave. The story that began with God coming to be with his people ends with God refusing to leave them.

He is with us, always.
